title: The Promise Was Not Made to the Strong
subtitle: On comfort, grass, and a renewal that is not a refill
teaser: Isaiah's most-quoted promise about renewed strength has a sentence in front of it that most readers skip: even the youths shall faint. The passage rules out the reading a tired person reaches for first, then makes an offer that only works if you have already run out.
theme: Renewal is promised to people already spent, and the running comes after the waiting.
framework: Isaiah 40:31 — they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength

modules.passage: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
emphasis: He giveth power to the faint
they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength
modules.scriptureContext: A promise that gets quoted at people with something left, and was written for people with nothing.

modules.definition: to wait, to look for, to hope — a waiting that leans toward something
modules.usage: This is the verb under "they that wait upon the Lord," and it is not the word for filling time until something better happens. Brown-Driver-Briggs connects it to a root meaning to bind together, perhaps by twisting, the way loose strands become a cord — though the lexicon prints that derivation with a "perhaps" attached, and it is worth holding as loosely as the lexicon does. What is not in question is the posture. The word turns up about forty-nine times in the Old Testament, and in nearly all of them somebody is leaning toward something they cannot yet see.

modules.heading: Who Was in the Room
modules.content:
Isaiah 40 opens the long second movement of the book, and it opens with the word comfort, said twice. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem. Her warfare is accomplished. That is the room this promise is spoken into — not a starting line, but the far end of an exile, addressed to people who have already been spent by it.

Which is why the verse immediately before it says what it says. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. That sentence removes the reading a tired person reaches for first — that renewal is what happens to people who had something in reserve. Youth is exactly what the passage disqualifies.

Then notice the order of what is promised. Mount up with wings as eagles. Run, and not be weary. Walk, and not faint. It descends. The spectacular thing comes first and the ordinary thing comes last, which is backwards from how anybody would build a sentence for effect — unless walking is the hardest of the three, and the one most of a life is actually made of.

And all three sit downstream of a single verb. They that wait. Not they that try again. Not they that press through. The strength here is renewed, which is a word for something being given back, and the condition attached to it is the one thing an exhausted person is least willing to do.

modules.prompt: Where are you being asked to keep going on strength you no longer have? Name the place plainly. Do not decide yet what to do about it.

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, You do not grow tired. We do. We have been running on what was left and calling it faithfulness. Teach us to wait on You before we ask You to bless our exhaustion. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: a prophet telling a comforted people they are grass, a Hebrew verb for renewal that means something closer to exchange, and a woman who wrote her best-known book from the bed she never got out of again.

modules.passage: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the Lord's hand double for all her sins. … The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
modules.scriptureContext: The ground the promise is standing on, and the prophet's own assessment of the people he has just been told to comfort.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A single weathered desert tree standing alone on open scrubland under a pale sky, rendered in deep blue and cream halftone.
modules.inlineImageCaption: One tree, still standing in country that gives it nothing. Isaiah 40 is addressed to people at that end of things — and the week the reading opens is going to spend most of its time in exactly this landscape.

modules.heading: Comfort, and Grass
modules.content:
The two halves of that passage do not sound like they belong to the same speaker.

First: comfort. Twice, which in Hebrew is how emphasis gets made. Speak tenderly. Tell her the hard service is finished, the debt is settled, it is over. That is the voice of somebody sitting on the edge of a bed.

Then, thirty seconds later, the prophet is told to cry out, asks what he is supposed to cry, and gets handed this: all flesh is grass. The grass withers. The flower fades. Surely the people is grass.

A modern editor would cut one of them. They read as contradictory — you comfort somebody, or you tell them they are vegetation, and it is difficult to see how you do both in the same breath. But the passage is not being cruel and it is not changing its mind. It is doing something more useful than either.

It is refusing to build the comfort on the people.

A comfort that depends on how much a person has left will hold exactly as long as their reserves do, which is to say it will fail on the day it is finally needed. So the prophet clears that ground first. You are grass. Everything you can generate is seasonal. The flower does fade, and the withering is not a moral failure — it is what grass does, and God, who made it, is the one saying so.

And then the sentence turns: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

That is what the rest of the chapter is built on, and it is why the promise at the end of it can be trusted by somebody with nothing in the tank. The comfort was never resting on the strength of the comforted. It is resting on the one thing in the passage that does not wither.

modules.definition: to pass on, pass away, change — and in this stem, to renew
modules.usage: The phrase in verse 31 is yachaliphu koach — they shall renew strength. Strong's gives the root as a primitive verb meaning "to slide by," and from there "to hasten away, pass on… or change." Brown-Driver-Briggs glosses it "pass on or away, pass through." It appears twenty-eight times in the Old Testament. In Isaiah 40:31 it is causative, and the lexicons render it there "change for better, renew," with strength as its object.
modules.usageNote: So the picture underneath the English is closer to changing than to filling. Not a tank topped up, which is what most readers hear in "renew," and which quietly implies the tank is the thing that matters. Something is passing on and something else is taking its place. Whatever a person had at the start of a hard season is not what carries them through it, and the passage is not promising that the old supply comes back.

wordByWord.meaning: those waiting on — a participle, an ongoing posture rather than a single act
they shall renew — causative; the strength is changed, not refilled
strength, power, capacity — the ordinary word for what a body has to give

relatedWords.meaning: weary, faint — the word the chapter keeps using, and it is applied to the young men and denied of God in the same passage

modules.content: The comfort was never resting on the strength of the comforted.

modules.heading: Eagles, Then Running, Then Walking
modules.content:
Read the three promises in the order they are given and something odd surfaces.

Mount up with wings as eagles. Then: run, and not be weary. Then: walk, and not faint.

Every instinct in a writer would reverse that. You build. You start with the walking and end on the wings, because that is where the applause is. Isaiah puts the wings first and finishes on a person putting one foot in front of the other.

The usual explanation is that the verse is describing a descent from spiritual highs to ordinary faithfulness, which is true enough as far as it goes but treats the ending as a consolation prize. There is a plainer reading available, and anyone in a long season already knows it: walking is the hardest of the three.

Flying is short. Running is measurable — it has a distance and a finish and somebody counting. Walking is the one that goes on. It is what a person does on the ordinary Tuesday of the fourth month of something that has no announced end, when there is no adrenaline in it, no audience for it, and no sense that any progress is being made. That is the condition the sentence closes on, and the promise attached to it is not that the walking will get easier. It is that the walker will not faint.

The other thing worth noticing is what all three share. None of them is a promise that the road shortens. Nothing here says the exile ends sooner, the body mends faster, or the load comes off. The whole promise operates on the person, not the circumstance.

Which is disappointing if you came for a different outcome, and enormous if you have been quietly wondering whether you can survive this one.

modules.heading: Where This Week Sits in the Story
modules.ancientTruth: This is the WILDERNESS stretch of God's story — the long middle, where a people are neither in bondage nor yet home, and where God does most of His teaching. Isaiah 40 speaks into the end of an exile: the hard service is finished, and the road home runs through desert. The chapter's own picture of the way back is a highway made straight in the wilderness.
modules.modernApplication: The modern version of that stretch is a season that has taken capacity away — health, energy, the ability to do the work you are known for — and has not yet given anything back. From inside it, that reads as punishment.
modules.connectionPoint: The week begins here on purpose, because the promise at the end of Isaiah 40 is the only kind that survives contact with real exhaustion: it is addressed to people who have already run out, and it does not ask them to find more.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Paul was given the same answer in fewer words, and he had asked three times to be spared: "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). And Jesus makes the invitation directly — "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" — which is Isaiah's promise with a face attached.

modules.heading: Renew Is Not a Word for Topping Up
modules.content:
Everything in this passage turns on what happens in the waiting, so it is worth being exact about what waiting is being asked for.

Start with what it is not. It is not passivity, and the Hebrew makes that hard to argue: qavah is a leaning word, a straining-toward. It is also not a technique for extracting something from God, which is how a great deal of religious waiting actually functions — a period of endurance performed in the hope that it will be scored and rewarded. Nothing in the sentence suggests that. The waiting is not what earns the strength. It is the posture in which the strength arrives, which is a different claim entirely.

And then there is the verb. English gives us renew, and renew sounds like restoration — the same thing, back again, at the level it used to be. That is what most people are actually praying for in a hard season. Give me back what I had. Let me be who I was in March.

The Hebrew is doing something else. Chalaph is a passing-on word, a changing word; the lexicons put its root sense at sliding by, passing through, and in the causative form here it means to change for the better. What is promised is not the retrieval of an old supply. It is a different supply.

That distinction sounds academic until you have prayed the first prayer for a long time. A person asking for their previous strength back is asking, without realising it, for the season to be undone. They are asking to be returned to the version of themselves who could carry that load — and the whole trouble is that the load has changed, and so has the body carrying it, and going backwards is not on offer.

What is on offer is stranger and better. Not the old strength restored, but strength that was never theirs to begin with, arriving on terms they did not set, in amounts they cannot audit in advance.

This is where the passage stops being encouraging and starts being difficult, because a person cannot verify that promise ahead of time. There is no way to check the tank. The only way to find out whether the strength is there is to still be walking tomorrow, and the only way to be walking tomorrow is to have waited today without proof.

Which is why the chapter spends its opening verses establishing that all flesh is grass. That is not pessimism. It is the removal of the alternative. If a person still believes there is something in reserve, they will spend the season looking for it, and they will find only the withering. The grass is not the enemy of the promise. It is the door into it.

modules.heading: The Book Written from the Bed
modules.content:
On 24 October 1931, Amy Carmichael was sixty-three years old and had been in south India for most of her adult life. She had arrived in 1895, founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in 1901, and built the thing she is remembered for out of unrelenting motion — travelling, rescuing children out of temple service, running a compound, writing at night.

That evening she stepped into an uncovered pit at a building site. She broke a leg, dislocated an ankle and injured her spine. She never fully recovered, and she spent most of the twenty years that remained to her confined to one room.

The part worth sitting with is what came out of that room. More than a dozen of her books were written after the fall, from the bed, by a woman in continual pain who had lost the only mode of working she had ever known.

One of them was Rose from Brier, published in 1933 — a book of letters written to the ill. And in it she says, plainly, why she did not wait until she was better to write it:

"But then the book would have been from the well to the ill, and not from the ill to the ill, which I think is what it is meant to be — a rose plucked straight from a brier."

Elsewhere in the same book she is more specific than most writers on suffering ever manage to be, because she is not describing a category. She is describing a Tuesday: "Has the day to be spent in bed? or in chair? or partly in both?"

And she is honest about who the letters are going to. "They go to some who are disappointed. They hoped to be well long ago and are not well yet."

She did not get her old strength back. The record is unambiguous about that; she did not walk out of that room. What she got instead was a different strength, on terms she had not chosen, and the work it produced has outlasted the work she was doing before the fall — which is the sort of thing that is only ever visible afterward, and is no comfort at all while the harrow is still moving.
modules.connectionToTheme: Carmichael is the passage in a person. The prayer that was not answered was the one asking for the previous capacity back. What arrived instead was the strength for a form of work she would never have chosen and could not have done standing up.

modules.heading: Plants That Only Grow There
modules.content: Spurgeon, writing about his own collapses in a lecture to men training for ministry, put the useful version of this in one sentence: "Some plants owe their medicinal qualities to the marsh in which they grow; others to the shades in which alone they flourish."
modules.historicalContext: Lectures to My Students, First Series (1875), Lecture XI, "The Minister's Fainting Fits" — a lecture he opens by admitting he speaks "by most painful experience." The claim is narrower than the inspirational use it usually gets: he is not saying suffering is good, and he does not say the marsh is pleasant. He says some things do not grow anywhere else.

modules.heading: What This Week Is Going to Ask
modules.content:
This is the first of seven readings, and it is worth saying at the start where they go, because the shape matters.

The week does not move from tiredness to energy. It moves from strength to attention.

Tomorrow the question becomes what is actually slowing a person down, and the answer in Hebrews turns out to be two different things that get treated as one — weight, which is not sin, and something that stands all the way around a runner. Wednesday is the pivot, and it is the bluntest day of the week: a prophet at the end of himself is given food and sleep before he is given a single word of explanation. Thursday is Martha, whose problem was never her hands. Friday is the sentence the whole week has been walking toward, which is about where the eyes go. Saturday gathers it. Sunday says almost nothing.

What holds it together is the thing Isaiah has already put in place today. The strength is not manufactured, and it is not retrieved. It is renewed, in the waiting, by somebody else — which means the practical question for the rest of the week is not how to get more of it. It is what a person is looking at while they wait.

That is not a small adjustment. Most advice for an exhausted person is about supply: sleep more, cut back, take something off the list. Some of that is right, and Wednesday will make the case for it more strongly than most readings would. But none of it answers the question of what to do on the day when the list has already been cut and the tiredness is still there.

Isaiah's answer, and the week's, is to look at something. Not to look away from the trouble — the prophet does not pretend the exile did not happen, and he calls the people grass to their faces. To look at the one thing in the passage that does not wither, and to keep looking, and to find that the walking continues.

modules.passage: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.
emphasis: you will find rest for your souls
modules.scriptureContext: Isaiah's promise with a face attached — and note that what is offered is not the removal of a yoke but the exchange of one.

modules.prompt: What have you been asking God to give back to you? Say it out loud, exactly as you have been praying it — and then ask whether you would recognise strength if it arrived in a form you had not asked for.
additionalQuestions: Isaiah tells a comforted people they are grass. Where in your life have you been trying to build the comfort on your own reserves?
Which of the three — flying, running, walking — is the one being asked of you right now?
What would waiting look like this week, if it were a posture rather than a delay?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: A breath prayer, taken straight out of verse 29. Six slow breaths, no more. It is not a technique and it is not meant to produce a feeling — the words do the work; the exercise is only holding still long enough to hear them.

steps.title: In
steps.description: Breathing in, silently: I have no might.

steps.title: Out
steps.description: Breathing out, silently: He giveth power to the faint.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.description: Six times, slowly. If the first half is hard to say, that is worth noticing rather than pushing past. Most people can admit tiredness. Fewer can admit having nothing left.

modules.heading: The Everlasting God Fainteth Not
modules.content:
The passage does not begin with the people. It begins with a question that sounds almost impatient: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard?

And then, before any promise is made to anybody, a description of God — the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth — with two verbs attached that are the same two verbs used of the young men a few lines later. He fainteth not, neither is weary.

That is the architecture of the whole thing. Weariness is the subject of the paragraph, and it is applied to everyone in it except one. The young men faint. The youths are weary. The people are grass. And standing outside that entire category, not because He is stronger but because He is of another kind altogether, is the one being waited on.

Which means the waiting in verse 31 is not a spiritual discipline in the abstract. It is a transfer of attention from a category that runs out to one that does not. A person waiting on the Lord is not primarily being patient. They are looking somewhere specific.

That is where the week is going, and it is why it is named for a strange little image: what happens when you look at the sun and then try to look at anything else. But that is Friday.

Today is only this. You are tired, and the tiredness is real, and Scripture agrees with you about the grass. And the one you are waiting on has never once been tired, has no searching of his understanding, and gives power to the faint — which is a category you may have spent a long time trying not to be in, and which turns out to be the only category the promise was ever addressed to.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: Everlasting God, You do not faint and You are never weary, and we have spent a long time trying to be like You in the wrong way. We have hidden the emptiness and called it strength. We are grass, and You said so first, and somehow that is a kindness. Do not give us back what we had. Give us what You give — power to the faint, in the amount You choose, on the day You choose it. Teach us to wait on You without calling the waiting wasted. And where we cannot fly or run, hold us up while we walk. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathing in: I have no might. Breathing out: He giveth power to the faint.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will stop asking for the strength I used to have, and start asking for the strength God is actually giving.
leavingAtCross: The belief that renewal means going back to who I was
The habit of hiding how little is left
The suspicion that being spent disqualifies me
receivingFromCross: A promise addressed to the faint, not to the fresh
Strength that arrives as a change rather than a refill
Permission to walk, on a day when flying is out of the question

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: Why does Isaiah say "even the youths shall faint and be weary" right before promising renewed strength?
options: To warn young people that they need God more than they think
To rule out the idea that renewal goes to those with something in reserve — the promise is for people already spent
To contrast Israel's weakness with the strength of surrounding nations
To explain why the exile happened
modules.explanation: The verse works by elimination. Youth is the best natural case anyone could make for having reserves, and Isaiah disqualifies it — the youths faint, the young men utterly fall. What remains is a promise that has nothing to do with how much a person started with, which is why the chapter first spends four verses establishing that all flesh is grass.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: The prophet of Isaiah 40
modules.era: eighth century BC, and possibly the sixth
modules.bio: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Chapter 40 begins a section that speaks as though the exile to Babylon has already happened, well over a century later — and scholars have long divided over what that means. The older reading takes it as Isaiah writing prophetically of a future he was shown. A widely held modern reading attributes chapters 40-66 to a later prophet or prophetic circle working in Isaiah's tradition. Both readings agree on what the chapter is doing and to whom.
modules.keyQuote: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
modules.lessonForUs: Whoever held the pen, the pastoral instinct is the same one running through the whole book: comfort that does not first tell the truth about grass is not comfort, it is flattery, and it will fail on the day it is needed most.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: The full opening of the chapter — comfort, the highway in the wilderness, the grass, and the shepherd who "shall gently lead those that are with young."
Paul asks three times and is refused three times, and is given a different answer than the one he requested.
"I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak." The same promise, in one line.
"In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat — for He gives sleep to His beloved."
"The LORD is good to those who wait for Him." Written by someone with no reason left to say it.

resources.title: Amy Carmichael, Rose from Brier (SPCK, 1933)
resources.description: Source of every quoted line in today's story, verbatim from the scanned text. Written from bed in the twenty-second month after her fall of 24 October 1931. Note: the widely quoted line about being "a fellow-toad under the harrow" is from the preface to her later Gold by Moonlight (1935), where she is describing this book — it is routinely misattributed to Rose from Brier itself.

resources.title: C. H. Spurgeon, Lectures to My Students, First Series (1875), Lecture XI
resources.description: Source of the line about plants and the marsh, verbatim. The lecture is "The Minister's Fainting Fits," and Spurgeon writes it out of his own recurring depression rather than about somebody else's. Free at archive.org.

resources.title: Hebrew data
resources.description: qavah (H6960) — "to wait, look for, hope"; about forty-nine Old Testament occurrences; BDB connects it to a root meaning to bind together, perhaps by twisting, and prints that derivation with "perhaps" attached. chalaph (H2498) — Strong's gives the root as "to slide by," hence "to hasten away, pass on… or change"; BDB "pass on or away, pass through"; twenty-eight Old Testament occurrences; in Isaiah 40:31 it is causative and the lexicons render it "change for better, renew."

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Isaiah 40 straight through in one sitting and mark every time weariness is mentioned. Then note which of those are said about people and which about God. The chapter's argument is almost entirely carried by that one distinction, and it is invisible if you start at verse 31 — which is where the verse is nearly always quoted from.
